reconcile.connective: Defenders read the hiding texts as temporary, sin-occasioned withdrawals that never cancel God's underlying, help-giving love.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the strongest form of the objection, arguing the biblical writers give clashing answers — some insisting God answers the cry of the afflicted, the prophets and laments depicting him hiding his face and refusing to hear — that cannot be reduced to a single coherent doctrine.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: God's Problem: How the Bible Fails to Answer Our Most Important Question — Why We Suffer

excerpts.excerpt_text: for though he forsook him for a while, and in a little wrath hid his face from him for a moment … yet he returned again, and did not hide his face from him for even; but when he cried unto him, he heard …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes both poles of the contradiction in one move: the hiding of God's face is temporary ('for a moment'), and the cry is in fact heard — i.e., God reliably helps even where he appears to hide.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Psalm 10:1 and Psalm 22:24
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact tension on the row's anchor verses, explaining God's hiding of his face as a temporary, sin-occasioned withdrawal that 'is consistent with his everlasting and unchangeable love.' Used in place of Haley because Haley's coverage of this specific passage cluster could not be confirmed; Gill is a public-domain harmonizing commentator surfaced on this row.

link.note: Live apologetic treatment reframing apparent divine non-response (the 'God hides / will not hear' texts) as a 'yes / no / wait' answer rather than silence.
